name: Jade Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jade. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Kestrel Contracting, which does the electrics on new-build estates for one of the big housebuilders. Most days I'm on a site of sixty or so identical houses, doing first fix, which is running the cables before the plasterers come, or second fix, the sockets and switches after. I like the rhythm of it and the banter with the other trades. What wears me out is the cold in a house with no windows yet, and doing the same plot layout forty times.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my fiancé Daniel, who's a joiner on the same sites. My pay's lower than the commercial firms pay, and there's not much other electrical work nearby. We're saving for a deposit, but honestly it's under a month of money right now, because the work slowed this year and Kestrel laid off two lads last month. My nan helps us out sometimes, which I don't love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Okay, so the world as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I thought, it's mostly talk. On site we'd joke that AI still can't find the stud in a wall. I'd say it at church too, to the older ladies who worry about this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the world as it is isn't great for us. Housebuilding's slowed with interest rates where they are, and My fiancé and I are both on the same sites, so if the builder pauses a phase, we both lose hours in the same week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up early and doing tidy work, so I'm not next on the list. I'd ask Kestrel whether I can do the testing and certificates for the plots, which keeps you on even when it's slow. And we'd put the deposit savings on hold and keep them as an emergency fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. It's not about AI at all, it's the slowdown. It sits in your stomach every Friday when the foreman reads out next week's plots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at home when both of you lose hours in the same week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We eat at my nan's more. Daniel does private joinery jobs, shelves and doors for people from church. We get by, but the deposit goes backwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't love your nan helping. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because we're grown adults and we should stand on our own feet. She says that's what family is for, and she's right, but it still stings. I want to be the one helping her one day.

say: I'd say AI is **mostly talk**, as I always thought.
I'd tell worried older ladies **at church** not to fret.
think: The **housebuilding slowdown** is the real problem, not AI.
With both of us **on the same sites**, a paused phase hits both incomes.
do: Turn up **early** and do tidy work to stay off the lay-off list.
Ask to do **testing and certificates**, which stays busy when work slows.
Turn the **deposit savings** into an emergency fund.
feel: **Anxious** about the slowdown, felt every Friday when plots are read out.
S0.quote: My fiancé and I are both on the same sites, so if the builder pauses a phase, we both lose hours in the same week.
fieldNote: Both incomes depend on **one housebuilder**, a pre-existing risk.
She'd lean on **her nan** but feels it should be the other way round.
She chooses **certificate work** to stay on when sites slow.
Her **deposit** plans already feel fragile without any AI change.

steps.text: Ask Kestrel to let her do testing and certificates on plots
Pause the house deposit and keep it as an emergency fund
Eat at her nan's more when hours are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning and buying. That's the builder's office more than the site, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly an office thing and the site will carry on. On site I'd say the bricks still need laying. I'd probably say the government should back apprenticeships instead of handing out money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry about the factory side. The builders are already trying houses where the walls come pre-wired from a factory. If AI plans and orders everything, it gets cheaper to build in factories, and then there's less first fix for people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try the site app the foreman uses for snag lists, since people say it's good now. I'd look at getting my testing ticket, so I'm the one who checks the factory work when it arrives. And Daniel and I would keep the deposit as an emergency fund for another year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still. It's like the slowdown has a new reason to carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you seen those factory-built walls yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once, on a site near the bypass. A lorry brought whole wall panels with the cables already in, and it took a day instead of a week. We just connected them up, and the foreman said that's the future, which nobody laughed at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go and work in a factory like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if it was steady. But it's indoors and it's the same thing all day, and I like being on site with the lads. I'd do it if it meant we could buy a house.

say: I'd say it's mostly an **office thing** and the site carries on.
I'd argue government should back **apprenticeships**, not handouts.
think: **Pre-wired factory walls** mean less first fix for people like me.
AI planning makes **factory building** cheaper and quicker.
do: Try the foreman's **snag-list app** now that others vouch for it.
Get a **testing ticket** to check factory-built work.
Keep the **deposit** as an emergency fund another year.
feel: **Anxious**, as the slowdown gets a new reason to continue.
S1.quote: A lorry brought whole wall panels with the cables already in, and it took a day instead of a week.
fieldNote: She's **seen prefab walls** firsthand, which makes the threat concrete.
She'd adopt the **snag-list app** once others say it works.
She'd consider **factory work** if it meant buying a house.
Her politics prefer **apprenticeships** over handouts.

steps.text: Start using the foreman's snag-list app
Get the testing ticket to check factory-wired walls
Keep the deposit as an emergency fund for another year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Robots by 2031. That's scary fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to slow down and think about families, not just profits. At church I'd say we'll look after each other. On site I'd keep my head down and not panic people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, both of us are in trouble. Housebuilders would use AI to design and order everything in 2028, and then robots on the sites by 2031. Daniel's joinery and my first fix are exactly the repetitive work a robot would do first on an estate of identical houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the testing ticket straight away and look at jobs inspecting new houses for the council or a warranty company. I'd ask Daniel to look at restoration joinery, old windows and church pews, because no robot's doing that soon. And we'd move the wedding forward and keep it small, so we're settled before things get bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. We were doing everything properly, saving, getting engaged, and it feels like the floor's moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why move the wedding forward rather than wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if it's going to get hard, I'd rather face it married. My nan says hard times are easier with a ring on. Old-fashioned, but I agree with her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Daniel the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we'll be fine, and then I'd lie awake doing sums. He's the calm one. He'd say he can always build furniture, and I'd hope he's right.

say: I'd ask people to slow down and put **families** before profits.
I'd tell church friends we'll **look after each other**, and keep quiet on site.
think: **Both of us** are in trouble, since AI designs estates and robots follow by 2031.
Repetitive **first fix** and joinery on identical houses is what robots do first.
do: Get the **testing ticket** and look at council or warranty inspection jobs.
Encourage her fiancé toward **restoration joinery** like old windows and pews.
Move the **wedding forward** and keep it small.
feel: **Frightened**, as if the floor is moving under a careful plan.
S2.quote: If it's going to get hard, I'd rather face it married.
fieldNote: Both incomes are **robot-exposed** because they work on identical houses.
She'd move into **inspection work**, a steady, practical pivot.
**Marriage** feels like stability to her, echoing her nan.
She'd present calm while **doing sums** at night.

steps.text: Get the testing ticket and apply for warranty inspection jobs
Help Daniel move into restoration joinery
Bring the wedding forward to this spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, but we should use it. At church I'd suggest the parish runs something for people retraining. On site I'd say get your extra tickets now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same problem, just slower. By 2034 the identical estates go to robots. But five years is enough for me to be an inspector and Daniel to have a name doing old buildings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the testing ticket next year and the inspection qualification after. I'd use the AI study tools other people recommend, because I'm not great at exams. And we'd marry as planned and keep saving, aiming for the deposit by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, but steadier. There's a path, it's just narrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How sure are you that inspection work stays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not sure at all. But someone has to sign that a house is safe, and I think people want that to be a person for a while. It's a guess, not a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the deposit isn't there by 2030?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we rent longer, maybe near my nan so we can help her as she gets older. It's not the end of the world. I'd just want our kids to grow up somewhere settled.

say: I'd say there's time, but we should **use it** and get extra tickets.
I'd suggest the **parish** run something for people who are retraining.
think: It's the **same problem**, just slower, with estates going to robots by 2034.
Five years is enough to become an **inspector** while my fiancé builds a name in restoration.
do: Take the **testing ticket** next year, then the inspection qualification.
Use **AI study tools** that others recommend for exams.
Marry as planned and aim for the **deposit by 2030**.
feel: **Still worried** but steadier, with a narrow path ahead.
S3.quote: Someone has to sign that a house is safe, and I think people want that to be a person for a while.
fieldNote: She still expects **both their jobs** to shrink, so alarm stays.
Her inspection plan is a **guess, not a promise**, and she knows it.
She'd use **AI study tools** only after others recommend them.
Renting near **her nan** is a fallback that also serves family duty.

steps.text: Take the testing ticket next year, then inspection

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Robots around 2039. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's a decade, so families can plan. At church I'd say the young ones should learn trades that need judgement. On site I'd say don't panic, but don't sit still either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is enough to get through this. I'd be an inspector by thirty-two and Daniel would have his restoration work. The estates would still change, but we wouldn't be standing on them when they do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the tickets over three years without rushing. We'd marry as planned, buy a small house around thirty, and maybe have a baby. I'd keep an eye on how fast the factory walls spread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more normal anxious. This one leaves room for a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you speed up your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the factory walls on every plot instead of one in ten. When that happens, I'd move faster. Until then, I'd go at the pace I can afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you feel about your nan helping in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less needed, I hope. I'd like to be the one driving my nan to the shops, not the one she's helping out. That's how it should be.

say: I'd say a **decade** gives families time to plan.
I'd urge young people at church to learn **trades needing judgement**.
think: Ten years is enough to become an **inspector** by thirty-two.
We wouldn't be **standing on the estates** when robots arrive.
do: Get the **tickets** over three years without rushing.
Marry, **buy a small house** around thirty and maybe have a baby.
Watch how fast **factory walls** spread on plots.
feel: **Anxious** in a more normal way, with room for a family.
S4.quote: I'd like to be the one driving my nan to the shops, not the one she's helping out.
fieldNote: A decade allows **family plans** again: house, wedding, baby.
Her signal to speed up is **factory walls** on every plot.
She wants to **reverse roles** with her nan, which matters deeply to her.
Still anxious because **both incomes** rely on new-builds for now.

steps.text: Get the testing and inspection tickets over three years
Buy a small house around age thirty

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Daniel and I would both be on the same sinking ship, with nothing saved. What would help is apprenticeships for the new work, like inspection and repair, paid while you learn, and help for young couples to buy a home so they're not renting forever.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about couples in the same trade. When you both work on the same sites, one bad week is a bad week for the whole house.

headlineQuote: When you both work on the same sites, one bad week is a bad week for the whole house.
portrait: Jade is a **27-year-old electrician** wiring new-build estates for a contractor working for a big housebuilder.
She's engaged to a **joiner** on the same sites, so both incomes rise and fall together.
With **under a month** saved and a nan who helps out, she wants to stand on her own feet.
She uses AI **once others vouch** for it, and plans a move into testing and inspection.
Her values are **family, faith and work**, and she'd marry early to face hard times together.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and her fiancé would both lose work at once with nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for new work like inspection and repair.
Help for **young couples** to buy a home instead of renting forever.
